Outbreak Investigation of E. Coli O157:H7 - Spinach (November 2021)
Outbreaks of Foodborne Illness
In this section
The FDA and CDC, in collaboration with state and local partners, investigated illnesses in a multistate outbreak of
E. coli
O157:H7. As of January 6, 2022, CDC declared this outbreak over.
FDA traced the supply chain for this positive product sample and deployed investigators to three farms in two separate states: California and Oregon. FDA conducted inspections, including sample collection and analysis, but inspections were limited because at the time the fields were fallow and no production activities were being conducted for spinach at any of the three farms. All samples collected were reported negative and no source or direct routes of contamination to the suspected spinach were found during the inspections. Investigators did report that one location processes product and sometimes uses product from multiple growers in one production run. This type of product co-mingling is not uncommon; but continues to present challenges for traceback investigations of foodborne outbreaks.
Recommendation
CDC announced the outbreak is over. There are no recommendations for consumers, retailers, or suppliers.

Title: CDC: Infant Botulism Outbreak Linked to Powdered Infant Formula (June 2026)

Product: Nara Organics Whole Milk Organic Infant Formula (recalled June 13, 2026).
Cases: 4 confirmed cases across 3 states, all hospitalized, no deaths. Status: Closed
investigation. Cause: Clostridium botulinum contamination.

Key Actions for Parents: Discard any recalled formula. Watch infants for symptoms (poor
feeding, loss of head control, difficulty swallowing) for up to a month. Seek immediate
medical care if symptoms appear.

For Healthcare Providers: Call the Infant Botulism Treatment and Prevention Program
(510-231-7600) immediately if botulism is suspected. Use BabyBIG (R) treatment without
waiting for lab confirmation. Report all suspected cases to state health departments.

question: Which groups are considered highest-risk for severe Listeria infection?

chunks.text:
Source: https://www.cdc.gov/listeria/about/index.html
Accessed: 2026-09-20
Title: CDC: About Listeria

Listeria are bacteria (germs) that can contaminate many foods. The infection is rare
but serious, though preventable through proper food safety practices.

At-Risk Populations: pregnant women, newborns, adults 65 and older, and immunocompromised
individuals face the highest risk. Other people can be infected with Listeria, but they
rarely become seriously ill.

Health Impact Statistics: the CDC estimates that annually in the United States, approximately
1,250 individuals contract Listeria, with roughly 172 deaths occurring. The infection
represents the fourth leading cause of death from foodborne illness nationally.

Illness Types: Listeria causes two categories, invasive illness and intestinal illness, each
presenting different symptoms depending on the infected person and affected body area.

Diagnosis and Treatment: laboratory testing identifies infection by growing Listeria from
body fluid or tissue samples. Treatment approaches vary -- those with intestinal illness
typically recover without antibiotics, while invasive illness cases require antibiotic
therapy. Dehydration prevention through fluid intake is recommended for diarrhea cases.

Prevention Strategies: know contamination-prone foods, follow food safety guidelines (Clean,
Separate, Cook, Chill), and monitor foodborne outbreak alerts and recalls through official
channels.

Consumption of food contaminated with
Lm
can cause listeriosis, a serious infection that primarily affects older adults, persons with weakened immune systems, and pregnant women and their newborns. Less commonly, persons outside these risk groups are affected.
Listeriosis can cause fever, muscle aches, headache, stiff neck, confusion, loss of balance and convulsions sometimes preceded by diarrhea or other gastrointestinal symptoms. An invasive infection spreads beyond the gastrointestinal tract. In pregnant women, the infection can cause miscarriages, stillbirths, premature delivery or life-threatening infection of the newborn. In addition, serious and sometimes fatal infections can occur in older adults and persons with weakened immune systems. Listeriosis is treated with antibiotics. Persons in the higher-risk categories who experience flu-like symptoms within two months after eating contaminated food should seek medical care and tell the health care provider about eating the contaminated food.

Title: CDC: Listeria Outbreak Linked to Meats Sliced at Delis

This outbreak is over. 61 cases, 60 hospitalizations, 10 deaths across 19 states.
Investigation started July 19, 2024; now closed.

General guidance distinguishes healthy people (who may have mild or no symptoms) from
high-risk groups -- pregnant people, newborns, adults 65+, and people with weakened immune
systems -- who face a much higher chance of severe illness including sepsis and meningitis.
Symptoms in high-risk groups can include fever, muscle aches, and headache, sometimes with
confusion, loss of balance, or convulsions when infection spreads to the nervous system.

Additional linked pages (Updates, Locations, Timeline) provide the state-by-state case
breakdown and the specific recalled deli meat brands and lot codes over the course of the
investigation.

Major Product Recalls
In this section
The FDA, along with CDC and state and local partners, are investigating a multistate outbreak of
Salmonella Senftenberg
infections linked to certain Jif peanut butter products produced at the J.M. Smucker Company facility in Lexington, Kentucky.
CDC’s review of epidemiological information indicates that five out of five people reported consuming peanut butter and four of the five people specifically reported consuming different varieties of Jif brand peanut butter prior to becoming ill. FDA conducted Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) analysis on an environmental sample collected at the Lexington, KY, J.M. Smucker Company facility in 2010. The analysis shows that this 2010 environmental sample matches the strain causing illnesses in this current outbreak. Epidemiologic evidence indicates that Jif brand peanut butter produced in the J.M. Smucker Company facility located in Lexington, KY, is the likely cause of illnesses in this outbreak.
J.M. Smucker Company has
voluntarily recalled
certain Jif brand peanut butter products that have the lot code numbers between 1274425 – 2140425, only if the first seven digits end with 425 (manufactured in Lexington, KY).
More information including advice for consumers, restaurants, and retailers is available at
